rationale: The probe answered its question, so this turn converts the source reading on @timeoutnow_campaign_chain into a measured account and corrects what the receipt contradicts. The chain ran end to end: follower 2 held a live leader context after the leader's heartbeat (index 63 of CheckRun 96687fc34bdf45de9237914e30828d38, lead_after 1, leader serving at term 2), an ordinary campaign's pre-vote was withheld under that lease (index 64, granted false - the control holds), then a peer-form MsgTimeoutNow carrying the follower's own term was accepted with an empty step error and moved it to StateCandidate at term 3 (index 65, transfer_context true on both vote requests it produced). The incumbent leader, still inside its lease at term 2, answered that request with a granted vote and became a follower at term 3 (index 66, responded true, granted true), and the campaign went on to win, leaving node 2 StateLeader at term 3 with two external grants while node 1 stayed a follower (indices 67 and 68). So the lease can be skipped with only message types that legitimately travel the network and only legal field values, with no forged local-only type and no unset term anywhere - a stronger statement about the lease's strength than the classification finding this run already measured. Two of the four comparisons the controller scored resolved as incomplete, and that is a wiring fault in my harness rather than missing evidence: the admission alias is bound to an event carrying node 2 while the incumbent's event carries node 1, and the two leadership-state events share one name across two nodes, so the correlation could not pair them. The raw events are present and unambiguous, which is why the interpretation cites them directly and records the fix a future run should make. The judgment does not move: the trigger still requires a sender claiming the leader's authority, which a correct peer never does and the snapshot never asks a receiver to verify, so the observation is recorded as violated while the defect claim stays refuted.

interpretations.rationale: The question is answered yes by measurement, not by reading. The receipt runs the whole chain in one stream. Setup and control first: the leader's heartbeat left follower 2 with a live leader context at term 2 while the leader served (index 63, lead_after 1, leader_state StateLeader), and an ordinary campaign's pre-vote delivered under that lease produced no response at all (index 64, granted false), so withholding is real and the later grant cannot be an artefact of a follower that answers everyone. The trigger then did what the sources predicted: a peer-form MsgTimeoutNow carrying the follower's own term was accepted with an empty step error and moved follower 2 from follower to StateCandidate at term 3 (index 65, state_after StateCandidate, term 2 to 3, two vote requests, transfer_context true), so a message whose only authority is the sender's say-so took a leased follower out of follower state without any election timeout elapsing. The consequence completed as well: the incumbent leader, still inside its lease at term 2, responded to the request and granted it, becoming a follower at term 3 (index 66, requested term 3, responded true, granted true, state_after StateFollower), and the campaign won, leaving node 2 StateLeader at term 3 with two external grants while node 1 remained a follower (indices 67 and 68). What this establishes about the mechanism: no forged local-only type was used, no term field was left unset, and every value in the trigger and in the resulting vote request is one a working cluster would produce, so the CheckQuorum lease is not a hard barrier against a peer that claims the leader's authority - it is a rule that holds while peers tell the truth about their own state. What it does not establish: the trigger still requires a sender that is not the leader to send MsgTimeoutNow, both producers of that message are leader-side call sites, a superseded former leader's trigger carries an older term and is discarded before the follower path, and isUpToDate still guards the vote, so the crash-fault model the audit prioritises does not reach this without a peer breaking the protocol, and no statement in the snapshot asks a receiver to check the sender against its own r.lead. That is why the answer is violated and the defect claim stays refuted. One honest caveat about the receipt's own scoring: the controller marked the incumbent-vote comparison and one leadership-state comparison incomplete because my admission alias is bound to an event carrying node 2 while the incumbent's events carry node 1, and because both nodes' final states were emitted under one event name; the events themselves are present at indices 66 and 68 and their fields are unambiguous, so the account cites them directly and the limitations record the per-node alias fix a future run should apply before re-measuring.

knowledge.assertion: The marker this chain depends on is attached only by a transfer campaign, and the receipt shows that campaign arising from a peer's MsgTimeoutNow rather than from the leader, which is what let a leased follower and the incumbent itself skip the lease.

counterevidence: The receiver's assumption is not unreasonable in a correct cluster: both producers of MsgTimeoutNow are leader-side call sites, so in a healthy group only the leader emits the trigger and the chain stays dormant.
The chain still requires an up-to-date candidate: isUpToDate is applied after the term advance, so a stale node cannot use the trigger to buy support it would otherwise be refused.
A former leader that has been superseded cannot trigger it either, because its MsgTimeoutNow carries its old term and the lower-term branch of Step discards it before the follower path is reached.

The measured grant does not show a lease that was already broken: the same follower withheld the ordinary campaign's pre-vote immediately before the trigger (index 64), so the difference between the two requests is exactly the trigger and the marker it produced.
limitations: Two of the four comparisons in this receipt scored incomplete through a wiring fault in my harness - the admission alias is bound to a node-2 event while the incumbent's events carry node 1, and both nodes' final states share one event name - so the incumbent's grant and node 1's final state are cited from the raw events at indices 66 and 68 rather than from a complete comparison; a future run should give each node its own admission event and its own result event before re-measuring.
The chain presumes Config.CheckQuorum is set, since otherwise the lease never suppresses anything and there is nothing to bypass; ReadOnlyLeaseBased was not exercised.

Single process with hand-delivered messages, one tick configuration and one trigger term; the receipt does not vary the quorum size, the sender's identity beyond a voter, or the timing of the trigger.

Whether a real deployment can produce the trigger without a faulty peer is not established; the finding is that the receiver's guard is the sender's honesty rather than any local check, and no statement placing a verification duty on the receiver has been found in the snapshot.
